controls.title: What you get, and what you control

items.title: Subtitles over the page
items.desc: Rendered in an isolated overlay that follows the video into fullscreen. Set the size and position, or show the original line under the translation.

items.title: Spoken translation
items.desc: On tiers that produce audio, you hear the translation while the original keeps playing behind it.

items.title: Keep, duck or mute the original
items.desc: One control from 0 to 100% over the original audio. While the translated voice speaks, the original ducks under it and comes straight back.

items.title: Your language, per session
items.desc: Choose what you want to hear and read each time you start. The spoken language is detected for you.

privacy.title: What it can and cannot see

items.title: One tab, chosen by you
items.desc: Only the tab you pressed the button on. Never your microphone, never another tab, never a background tab.

items.title: No access to your browsing
items.desc: The extension does not request access to all sites. No access to your tabs, history, cookies or network requests.

items.title: The page itself is never sent
items.desc: Not the URL, not the title, not the video id, not the page content. Only the audio, the language you chose and your session token.

items.title: AI-generated, and it says so
items.desc: Subtitles and any translated voice are generated by AI and can be wrong. The voice is synthesized — it is not a recording of the speaker.

limits.title: What it does not do
limits.subtitle: The things worth knowing before you install it, rather than after.

items.title: Chrome only
items.desc: Firefox, Safari and Edge are not supported, and we do not claim otherwise.

items.title: Web clients, not desktop apps
items.desc: It listens to a browser tab, so the Google Meet and Zoom desktop applications are out of scope.

items.title: A few pages take no subtitles
items.desc: Chrome forbids injecting scripts into its own pages and the Web Store. Audio translation still runs there; the overlay does not appear.

items.title: One language detection per session
items.desc: The spoken language is detected when you press start. A video that switches language halfway through is not re-detected — restart the session.

items.title: No latency figure
items.desc: We have not measured translation delay on the shipped build, so we do not publish a number for it. It varies with the tier, the language pair, your device and your network.

billing.title: Same account, same balance
billing.desc: The extension bills the VoxTranslate credits you already have, per minute of speech — from $0.0045 per minute, per language. New accounts start with $2 of credit and no card.

items.q: Does it work with Google Meet and Zoom?
items.a: With their web clients, yes. VoxTranslate listens to the audio of a browser tab, so Google Meet Web and Zoom Web work. The desktop applications do not, because there is no browser tab to listen to.

items.q: Can it translate a YouTube live stream?
items.a: Yes. A live stream is audio playing in a tab, and that is what VoxTranslate translates. Subtitles appear over the player as the stream runs, with no waiting for a recording.
No. It captures the audio of one browser tab — the one you started it on. There is no microphone access anywhere in the extension, and it never requests one.

items.q: Can I still hear the original audio?
items.a: Yes. The original keeps its own volume control, from 0 to 100%. When the translated voice speaks, the original ducks underneath and comes back as soon as it stops.
Chrome only. Firefox, Safari and Edge are not supported. The extension uses Chrome's tab-capture and side-panel APIs, which the others do not provide in the same form.
No. It draws on the credit balance in your VoxTranslate account, billed per minute of speech. Every new account starts with $2 of credit and no card, which is enough to try it properly.

perLanguage.title: How billing works
perLanguage.body: You are billed as a listener, at the rate of the engine YOU chose — you pay for the quality you asked for, not for whatever anyone else picked. The meter runs only while someone else is speaking a language different from yours, and counts one stream for each person doing so at that moment.
perLanguage.example: If everyone in the room already speaks your language, nothing is translated and nothing is charged. In a webinar, the host's organisation pays — attendees never do.

items.q: Who pays — the speaker or the listener?
items.a: The listener. You are billed for the translation you receive, at the rate of the engine you chose, and only while someone is actually speaking a language different from yours. Talking is free; having it translated for you is what costs. Webinars are the exception: there the host's organisation pays and attendees never do.

items.q: Why is the rate sometimes multiplied?
items.a: Each person speaking a language different from yours is a separate live translation stream. One foreign speaker costs the rate; three talking over each other cost three times it, for as long as they overlap. The moment nobody is speaking a foreign language, the meter stops.
No. Credits are pay-as-you-go and do not expire monthly. Business and Enterprise plans exist for teams that want shared credits and administration, not because per-minute use requires them.

items.q: What does the free starter credit include?
items.a: Every new account gets $2 of credit, usable on any engine. On Standard that is several hours of translated speech.

items.q: Can I use it inside Google Meet or Zoom?
items.a: Yes. The VoxTranslate browser extension translates the audio playing in your tab, which covers Meet and Zoom on the web, alongside the built-in VoxTranslate call and webinar rooms.
